records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no atomic SET match_count = match_count + 1 and no locking, so concurrent validations lose increments. Two users signing up with the same blocked email simultaneously each read match_count=5 and both write 6, undercounting the block statistics the table exists to collect; the counter permanently drifts from reality.
records.rationale:
In the newly added `BlockedEmail.should_block?` method, the diff shows a classic read-modify-write pattern without atomic increment or locking:

```rb
record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first
if record
  record.match_count += 1
  record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now
  record.save
end
```

Under concurrent validations for the same email, two threads/processes can read the same `match_count` and both write back `+1`, losing an increment. This is a real correctness defect in the statistics being tracked (`match_count` and potentially `last_match_at`).

Two users signing up with the same blocked email simultaneously each read match_count=5 and both write 6, undercounting the block statistics the table exists to collect; the counter permanently drifts from reality.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)) with no downcasing anywhere in BlockedEmail, while User normalizes stored emails, so a blocked_emails row loaded with mixed-case case never matches. Operators who bulk-load the table with 'Bad@Spam.org' get zero blocks for users whose canonical email is bad@spam.org; the block list silently fails for any non-lowercase row.
records.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does a direct equality lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) with no normalization (no `downcase` in BlockedEmail or in the new EmailValidator before calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`). On typical DBs (e.g., Postgres) string equality is case-sensitive, so a `blocked_emails.email` stored as `Bad@Spam.org` would not match an attempted email `bad@spam.org`, causing the block list to be bypassed for mixed-case rows.

Callers doing `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) == false` or logging the raw value get nil and mis-handle it; in Ruby this is latent, but any future consumer comparing explicitly gets silently wrong control flow.
records.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `should_block?` ends with `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, which returns `nil` when no record is found (i.e., `record` is `nil`). records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})")` by naively interpolating the raw comma-separated setting, so a blacklist of 'mail.ru, spam.com' produces a regex matching '@(mail[.]ru, spam[.]com)' as a single literal alternation-free pattern with the comma embedded. This is carried over from the deleted User#email_in_restriction_setting?, but the diff re-homes the broken parser into a shared validator, entrenching it: any site setting with more than one domain never matches anything (whitelist) or never blocks anything (blacklist), and the next fix now has to change the new validator's public behavior.
